extracted.intended_audience: fiction and creative writers conducting field research
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writers on planning and conducting field research (site visits, expert interviews, sensory observation) to gather authentic details for fiction/worldbuilding. Covers preparation, methods for capturing sensory detail, working with experts, and ways to convert raw experience into usable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do thorough prep research before you go
rubrics_metrics.description: Do a ton of research before I go, so that I’m not asking the stupid 101 questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background work prevents wasting experts' time and lets you ask specific, useful questions. Use preparatory reading to identify the area of information you need (what effects you’re after) rather than expecting to learn foundational material in the field trip itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and recruit experts; offer an honorarium
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify an expert who can help you. Offer an honorarium (even a small sum) to signal seriousness and secure their help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pay $150 to an expert who will take you to relevant sites, introduce you to other specialists, and point out salient details. If you’re junior or context-appropriate, a coffee or modest gesture can be an appropriate honorarium. Experts shift your lens and point out what matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer honorarium to buy seriousness not just time
rubrics_metrics.description: What you are paying for with $150 or $200 is not their time. You are buying their belief that you are serious about this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small monetary offer often convinces experts to invest effort and take you on guided visits. The amount is flexible depending on career stage and context; alternative tokens (meals, coffee) can suffice for some contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and plan for unknown unknowns (Howard's realm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the framework: known knowns, known unknowns, things you don’t know that you know, and unknown unknowns. Acknowledge upfront that you’ll encounter unknown unknowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that you may need to ask 'stupid' questions; reclassify surprises into known unknowns and follow up. This mindset prepares you for the iterative expansion of questions while researching (e.g., one question can turn into a hundred).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experts to target relevant, non-obvious details
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts will tell you which sites, people, and small details are worth investigating and how insiders see things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts introduce you to useful contacts and help you notice details you would otherwise miss; they help you 'shift your lens' to view things as insiders do (e.g., which fossil sites matter, which practitioners are worth interviewing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Walk places with a writing mindset to notice small, convincing details
rubrics_metrics.description: Walk down the street thinking 'I’m going to have to describe this someday; what are the little details that can convince a reader of the large details.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, accurate details persuade readers to assume larger realities; you don't have to visit exact locales (e.g., Paris) — noticing particular real features of a local building/café can be sufficient for verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture broad sensory details (sight, sound, smell, touch/temperature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t just write down what things look like—get the sounds, smells, how it feels (e.g., stepping from air-conditioning into heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensory specifics (smells like smoky mildew; feeling of cramped quarters) are often the most evocative. Record transitions and bodily reactions as they help convey emotion without telling the reader how to feel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do freewriting on site to bank sensory impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Go someplace and write for half an hour without letting your fingers stop moving to capture sensory details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise captures raw impressions that you can mine later for narration. It’s a recommended formal exercise for students and a practical note-taking method for fieldwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use photos but don’t let the camera replace direct observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Your camera captures different things than your eyes; photo-documenting is useful, but remember to look beyond the lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take photos, then later study them to notice details you missed in person. Combine photos with on-site freewriting and breathing/reflecting in the place to get a fuller sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: After photographing, re-describe photos from a character’s POV
rubrics_metrics.description: Take pictures, then go back, look for things in the pictures your eyes didn’t notice and describe them as if a character is noticing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This homework turns photographic evidence into narrative detail: teach your eyes to see what the camera recorded and translate that into sensory, character-focused description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analog field research when direct access is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can’t go to the exact place you need, find narrow analogs (e.g., a narrow street for a European lane, a local cemetery for another one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analog experiences let you simulate certain physical or sensory conditions you need to write convincingly without expensive travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do targeted visual-reference research and develop shorthand/iconic visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: For visual elements (e.g., simple silhouettes for game cards or creature designs), research images, clip art, and references to find shapes that read instantly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Howard’s anecdote: finding a whale silhouette involved hours of research; the right simplified image may require extensive reference work to avoid unintended associations (e.g., shaping more like a shark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical details to convey emotion rather than telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey how someone feels by describing physical conditions and embodied reactions so the reader can come along for the experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cramped submarine cabins imply discomfort; smoky mildew smell evokes memory; describe what a character is noticing instead of stating emotions outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect an iterative process: get feedback and refine accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Field research and draft accuracy improve by iteration—show drafts to specialists (e.g., fighter pilots) and incorporate corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You’ll rarely get everything right first try; experts can point out remaining errors and help you narrow unknown unknowns into fixable known unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note-taking methods mix: freewriting, photos, shorthand, and follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a combination of methods—freewriting, photographs, shorthand sketches/icons, and scheduled follow-ups with experts—to capture and refine research material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different media capture different information; plan to synthesize them later. Bring devices (phone/camera), but also commit to on-site writing and later contact experts for clarification.
